title: "Be," and it is
hook: His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say be, and it is (36:82)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ya-Sin's moon, returning like an old date stalk. Your line was each swims in its orbit.

A man walks up holding an old bone, dry and crumbling, picked up from some forgotten grave. He crushes it in his fist, and the dust falls between his fingers. Then he asks the question that's been his whole argument: who could bring this back to life? Anyone who's stood at a funeral has asked a version of it. Surah Ya-Sin ends by answering him, and the answer comes down to a single word of two letters in Arabic.

Verse seventy-eight. He coins a comparison for Us, Allah says, and forgets his own creation. He asks, who will revive bones once they've rotted away? Verse seventy-nine answers: the One who brought them into being the first time will revive them. He knows every creation. The man forgot that he himself was once nothing. If starting a person from nothing was possible, starting again from dust is no harder. Verse eighty adds a picture: the One who makes fire for you from the green tree. Something living and wet, and out of it comes flame. Then the line the whole surah has been walking toward. Pickthall: "But His command, when He intendeth a thing, is only that He saith unto it: Be! and it is." In Arabic: kun, fa-yakun. Kun is two letters, kaf and nun. Muslims understand this as the Qur'an's way of describing Allah's power, not a picture of Allah speaking like a person: no effort, no delay, no materials needed. The Qur'an uses the phrase in several places: for the creation of the heavens and earth, for the birth of 'Isa, Jesus, and here, for raising the dead. Then the last verse of Ya-Sin: glory to Him in whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you'll be brought back. This is why the surah is read beside the dying. The question in that room is the man's question: can this come back? Ya-Sin's answer is the first answer again: the One who began it from nothing can begin it again.

In the verse, there's no gap between the command and the thing; a life is full of gaps. Think of one task you've been putting off, a call, a form, an apology, and picture only its very first step, small enough for a minute. If you pray, you can say bismillah over it, and sit quietly with the decision made.
Be. Kun, the word of Allah's command in Ya-Sin's closing verses: He says to a thing be, and it is, and so He can raise the dead. Today's word.
Your line: no harder the second time. Two letters, kaf and nun. That's day five hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims often say 'kun fa-yakun' when speaking of Allah's power to bring about what seems impossible, and the closing verses of Ya-Sin are commonly recited at funerals and by the dying.

chat.says: How does Ya-Sin answer the man asking who could bring old bones back?
